newsitem.title: USA: NYS MCCALL OPPOSES $425 MLN BOND SALE FOR STADIUMS.
newsitem.headline: NYS MCCALL OPPOSES $425 MLN BOND SALE FOR STADIUMS.

text.p: The New York State Comptroller on Wednesday said he supported plans for a big school bond but opposed a much smaller debt sale for stadiums because the state's voters would not get to decide if it were needed.

H. Carl McCall said, "That will not be taken to the public. That's again a continuation of back-door borrowing, of the legislature doing this without public consent, and I'm opposed to that. I think that is a practice that we have to stop."
He made the comments during an interview with RFTV that will be aired later Wednesday.

New York State's new, $68 billion budget for fiscal 1998 includes a plan to sell $425 million of bonds to help create jobs by building stadiums, like the Sportsplex center on Coney Island, as well as cultural and other projects designed to attract tourists.

In contrast, McCall, who was seen as the strongest Democrat candidate in next year's gubernatorial race until he recently decided to instead seek re-election as comptroller, said he favored a planned $2.4 billion school bond.

He explained that he supported this much bigger debt sale in part because it will be on the ballot in November. And McCall also stressed the urgent need to repair the state's public schools. "There's no question that through-out the state we have a very serious degree of deterioration in our public schools and we have to provide an adequate learning environment for our children."

However, Albany's lawmkers should tell voters what specific projects the school bond would pay for, McCall said. "What I find unfortunate about the bond issue is that it does not specify how that money will be used. It would be better if we had some idea of what will be the criteria, what kinds of schools will be fixed, in what areas geographically. I think we would have a better chance of convincing the public to support the issue if they have some idea of how the money is going to be used."

A spokesman for the state Department of Education said that if voters approve the school bond referendum, its officials will select specific projects based on the criteria the legislature will set when it resumes sessions, probably this autumn.
